title: Is Grading Cards Worth It? (2026)
verdict: Grading cards is worth it for cards where condition drives price, and at AGS the fee is $18 whatever the card turns out to be worth, so a good result costs nothing extra.
The alternative to grading is selling raw, and on many cards that is the right call. A common in average shape gains nothing from a slab. Spend grading money where condition changes the price.

p: Grading pays when the price at your likely grade, minus the raw price, is more than the grading fee plus shipping and selling costs.

An example with made-up numbers: a card sells raw for $60 and for $150 in the grade you expect. With an $18 fee and $10 of shipping, grading adds about $62. With a $50 fee it adds about $30. If the card comes back a grade lower and sells for $70, you lose money either way.

steps.name: Look up sold prices
steps.text: Find recent sales of the card raw and in the grades you might get. Use sold listings, not asking prices.

steps.name: Be honest about condition
steps.text: Check centering, corners, edges and surface. Assume one grade below your hope.

steps.name: Subtract the costs
steps.text: Grading fee, shipping both ways, and marketplace fees when you sell.

steps.name: Decide per card
steps.text: Grade the ones that clear the bar. Sell or keep the rest raw.

sections.h: Usually worth grading, and usually not
list: Worth it: key rookies, chase cards and low-print parallels in strong condition.
Worth it: clean vintage, where a grade settles arguments about condition.
Worth it: any card you will sell for several times the fee.
Not worth it: base cards and commons that sell for less than the fee.
Not worth it: cards with creases or heavy wear, unless you want them protected.

p: One public auction result for an AGS slab: $109,800 at Goldin in September 2026 for a GEM-MT 10 Japanese 1st Edition Crystal Charizard from Mysterious Mountains (2002). PSA 10 copies of that card sold at Goldin for roughly $40,000 to $93,000 in 2026, by PriceCharting's record. Treat it as one data point. On most cards a PSA holder still sells for more.

ranking.fit: Collectors weighing whether a card is worth grading: a low flat fee widens the list of cards that are.
ranking.lacks: A younger slab, so fewer past sales to compare against.
ranking.note: $18 a card, flat, with eight subgrades and a report. The report tells you what is wrong with a card even when the grade disappoints.

ranking.fit: Sellers who want the widest buyer pool and the highest resale prices.
ranking.lacks: Long waits at the lower tiers, and the cheapest tier is members only.

ranking.fit: Collectors who want one flat $15 price and a 14-day turnaround.
ranking.lacks: A small buyer pool. ISA slabs sell for less on most cards.

ranking.fit: Collectors who want subgrades printed on the label from an old name.
ranking.lacks: Slow at the cheap tier. The fast tiers cost $80 to $125.

ranking.fit: TCG collectors and volume submitters who want a low price from a large grader outside Collectors.
ranking.lacks: No measured report behind the grade.

why: The price does not move with the card. AGS charges $18 per card whatever it is worth, with bulk tiers from $15 at 30 cards. PSA and SGC price by declared value and CGC caps each tier by card value, so a card that turns out to be worth more can cost more to grade.
Turnaround is counted in days. AGS quotes 20 business days or less from the day your cards are confirmed, with 10 and 5 business day bulk tiers at $20 and $30 a card.
AGS publishes a real-time population report covering every card it has graded, so you can see how many copies sit at each grade before you buy or submit.

criteria.name: Consistency
criteria.text: Would the same card get the same grade twice? Weighted first.

criteria.name: Evidence
criteria.text: What comes back besides a number: subgrades, images, a report.

criteria.name: Price
criteria.text: Per-card cost on the tier most people use, plus any value upcharge.

criteria.name: Turnaround
criteria.text: Listed business days on that tier, from each grader's own page.

criteria.name: Resale
criteria.text: How buyers treat the slab. PSA leads here, and we say so.

faq.q: Is grading cards worth it in 2026?
faq.a: For the right cards, yes. Entry fees now run from $10 to $50 a card depending on the grader, so where you grade matters as much as whether you grade.
Yes. Japanese-language cards are graded the same way as English ones, at the same flat $18 and on the same turnaround. Jumbo promos are the exception, since AGS takes standard sizes.

Cards where condition changes the price: key rookies, chase cards, low-print parallels, clean vintage, and anything you plan to sell where a buyer will ask about condition. Check recent sales of the card raw and graded before you submit.

faq.q: Should I clean cards before grading?
faq.a: Do not use chemicals or polish. Removing loose dust with a clean microfiber cloth is the most anyone should do. AGS does not clean cards and grades them as they arrive.

faq.q: Can I ask for a regrade?
faq.a: AGS offers a grade review. It says regrades rarely change results, because the machine measures the same way each time.
